evidence.note: Fictional droid fighters illustrate the accountability problem for autonomous weapons.

segments.question: Should the US Navy replace all its crewed aircraft with drones?
segments.answerShort: A mixed force keeps people available to make decisions where the data are unreliable or lethal force is at stake.

segments.title: If Warspite could carry later memories into Jutland
segments.body: The machine-spirit premise gives the First World War Warspite memories from a later ship of the same name. One possibility is that the two already share a spirit, which leaves open what new knowledge would reach Jutland or what difference it would make.

evidence.note: The machine-spirit premise is a playful counterfactual.

segments.question: What would change at Jutland if a later Warspite could pass its memories to the earlier battleship?
segments.answerShort: What Warspite would do differently is left open, and the German fleet is expected to see little change.

segments.title: A Bolshevik revolution after the Russo-Japanese War
segments.body: The scenario brings a Lenin-led revolution forward to the aftermath of the Russo-Japanese War. An earlier revolution could alarm the Kaiser, whose later wartime interest in revolutionary Russia is described as a means to win the war. France might intervene or seek alignment with Britain and Japan. Japan's opportunity would depend on how soon the instability followed the fighting.

evidence.note: An earlier Russian revolution and possible responses by Germany, France and Japan.

segments.question: What if a revolution like October 1917 took place in Russia after the Russo-Japanese War?
segments.answerShort: It could invite German intervention, leave France looking for allies and give Japan a chance to advance farther.

segments.title: Admiral Gorshkov and the trade between firepower and endurance
segments.body: A frigate that expects support nearby can devote more of its space to weapons. British, American and French ships are more likely in this comparison to carry spares and stores for distant operations. There is also a choice between carrying another missile and spending more on computing and targeting to improve the odds of a hit on the first shot.

evidence.note: The opening wording is unclear. The comparison concerns carried weapons, targeting and supplies for distant deployments.

segments.question: Why do ships such as Admiral Gorshkov appear heavily equipped for their tonnage?
segments.answerShort: Operating within reach of support can reduce the space needed for stores and leave more for weapons.

segments.title: Concrete training bombs and collateral damage
segments.body: Concrete training bombs are considered as a way to limit collateral damage in a strike on a terrorist target. Existing training stocks could make such bombs available in quantity. Comparable use elsewhere is mentioned. Reports conflict on whether the US Air Force used them in the operations at issue.

evidence.note: Training stocks and reported precedents make the idea plausible. The particular US use remains unconfirmed.

segments.question: Are US aircraft using concrete training bombs for urban strikes to reduce collateral damage?
segments.answerShort: The idea is considered plausible, but the accounts are conflicting and the claim remains unconfirmed.

segments.title: Land-attack missiles for a Type 212 without vertical launch cells
segments.body: Without vertical cells, compatibility with the submarine's other launch arrangements matters. Tube-launched Tomahawk is described as a past capability with limited availability. A missile for Turkey's Type 214 comes up before attention turns to the Norwegian option. IDAS is also mentioned in connection with the submarine family.

evidence.note: The Canadian purchase is a premise. Missile-development names and status are uncertain.

segments.question: What land-attack weapon could Canada use if it fielded a Type 212 without vertical launch cells?
segments.answerShort: A weapon being adapted to the Type 212 family appears the likeliest choice, with a submarine-launched Naval Strike Missile suggested.

segments.title: How the war in Ukraine affected Royal Navy drone plans
segments.body: The Royal Navy was exploring drones before the war, so adoption of uncrewed systems was plausible in either scenario. The war is seen as a reason for a stronger commitment. How much work would pass from crewed ships to large uncrewed vessels remains open.

evidence.note: Earlier drone work and the war's effect on adoption. The precise platform and role in the prompt are unclear.

segments.question: Would the Royal Navy have pursued large uncrewed surface vessels without the war in Eastern Europe?
segments.answerShort: Work on drones had already started, so the general direction was likely even without the war.

segments.title: 28- and 30-pounder long guns in the age of sail
segments.body: Lighter 9- and 12-pounders provide a comparison for proportions. A standard 32-pounder is already long and heavy. Making a heavy gun even longer increases the cost and, in the example given, risks a burst gun.

evidence.note: The 28- and 30-pounder examples are recalled without names. The costs and risks of extra length are illustrated with a 32-pounder.

segments.question: Were there 28- or 30-pounder long guns in the age of sail?
segments.answerShort: Both weights are recalled as having been tried and used, although no examples are named.

segments.title: Reginald Henderson and the Type 45 in 2001
segments.body: The scenario gives Henderson about a year to learn whom to approach and which procedures could change a decision. His earlier handling of HMS Unicorn as an aircraft support ship illustrates why procurement categories mattered. For Type 45, he would press the Admiralty to explain what the destroyer would do after it expended its missiles and who could justify assuming it would still be safe.

evidence.note: HMS Unicorn illustrates Henderson's handling of procurement categories. A Type 45 with an empty magazine is the counterfactual test.

segments.question: What might Admiral Henderson have done if he arrived in 2001 before major Type 45 decisions?
segments.answerShort: He would first have to learn modern politics, then could press the Admiralty to justify the destroyer's missile capacity.

segments.title: Hypersonic launch cells for Canada's River-class destroyers
segments.body: Installing the cells in an existing hull means removing other equipment. A new section raises questions about buoyancy, fuel, redundancy and survivability, as well as construction costs and timing. The launchers would occupy only part of that section, and the rest would have to justify its length and weight. Fire control, sensors, maintenance access and personnel would also be needed. A fit on only four ships makes it harder to keep a missile ship available.

evidence.note: Displaced capabilities, the effects of adding a hull section and the systems a four-ship installation would need.

segments.question: What would it mean for Canada to fit River-class destroyers with the kind of hypersonic launch cells going into Zumwalt?
segments.answerShort: The launchers would have to justify what they displace. Adding a hull module would carry its own construction and integration costs.

segments.title: A Canadian destroyer squadron for conventional deterrence
segments.body: Dedicating four of twelve ships to conventional deterrence would leave eight ships to cover work planned for twelve. Even with all fifteen hulls, four strike ships would make up more than a quarter of the class. Forward basing in the Arctic would give them a different role and level of protection from keeping them nearer home. Ordinary refit schedules could leave all four unavailable at once. The alternative adds five hulls for four squadrons of five, with one squadron assigned to deterrence. Keeping the original production facilities active could reduce the additional cost.

evidence.note: The four-ship proposal risks simultaneous unavailability. The alternative adds five hulls to the fifteen-ship programme. The cost figures and their scope need confirmation.

segments.summary: Four dedicated missile ships could pull a substantial share of the River class away from regular escort work.

segments.title: Comparing American and Chinese warship production
segments.body: Chinese yards are assessed to be building more ships overall, with smaller vessels contributing more to their total. The gap looks different if the count is limited to larger warships. US production fell for a period, and a steadier run of Arleigh Burke destroyers is cited as part of its recovery. The comparison depends on which ships are counted and whether yards can sustain the rate.

evidence.note: Qualitative comparison of ship mix and Arleigh Burke production, without output figures.

segments.summary: Hull counts give only part of the picture when the US and China build different mixes of ships.

segments.title: Type 45 costs if Type 23 production had kept the yard active
segments.body: The estimate concerns the first ships of the class. A yard moving directly from one order to the next would have started on Type 45 with an active production line. A lower price might have allowed two batches of four, with a third batch floated as a possibility. Keeping the yard active could also have made it available for carrier construction.

evidence.note: The £100 million is a counterfactual estimate. The accounting basis is unclear in the captions.

segments.question: If the full Type 23 order had kept the yard active, would the Type 45 have cost less and would the Royal Navy have bought more?
segments.answerShort: A continuous workload might have saved roughly £100 million on initial work and made an eight-ship order more plausible.

segments.title: The Lynx, Hind and Apache as personal helicopter choices
segments.body: The Lynx choice comes from a favourable impression of the aircraft. The panel initially guesses Black Hawk while any military helicopter is eligible. The Apache is preferred once the choice is limited to attack helicopters. One participant has flown in an Apache. The participant who chose it has yet to do so.

evidence.note: The caption forms for Hind and Lynx are imperfect. The participants distinguish general and attack-helicopter preferences.

segments.question: Which military helicopters would the participants choose to own?
segments.answerShort: The questioner picks the Mi-24 Hind, while the panel names the Westland Lynx and AH-64 Apache.

segments.title: The appearance of the FDI and Mogami frigates
segments.body: The FDI's profile wins a personal comparison that also considers larger frigates such as Type 26. The Mogami appeals for a different reason, since its shape is seen to follow its function.

evidence.note: FDI and Mogami are identifiable. One other design name is garbled.

segments.question: Which modern frigate design is the most attractive?
segments.answerShort: The FDI is picked for its looks, and the Mogami is admired for the way its shape follows its function.

segments.title: What might follow China's Type 055 destroyers?
segments.body: Type 055 is described as occupying a role between destroyer and cruiser, with Type 052D in the middle of the fleet. A Type 052D follow-on could become the main destroyer built in numbers. Type 055B and Type 055C are floated as possible labels for a larger follow-on, depending on whether the second batch already received a suffix. New technology requiring a redesign is one possible reason for a pause. Some reports of new hulls could concern uncrewed systems. The order of the programmes remains open.

evidence.note: Possible roles for Type 052D and Type 055 successors, batch naming and uncertainty about the programme sequence.

segments.question: What might China build after the Type 055 destroyers?
segments.answerShort: A replacement for the more numerous Type 052Ds could come first. A larger ship might eventually follow Type 055.

segments.title: A modern Royal Navy at First World War scale
segments.body: The hypothetical uses the First World War fleet as a benchmark for numbers while keeping modern ships. Supporting that many modern vessels would strain the Treasury. The fleet mix and total cost remain open.

evidence.note: The short answer is a joke about the Treasury that points to the cost of expansion.

segments.question: What if the modern Royal Navy had as many ships as it did at its First World War peak?
segments.answerShort: The immediate objection is the cost of supporting that many modern ships.

segments.title: Royal Navy budget and crewing constraints
segments.body: A larger fleet would need more funding and more people to crew the ships. The government faces difficult choices about the fleet, with no specific option identified here. The officers, non-commissioned officers and sailors already serving are assessed favourably. The concern is that there are too few of them for the Navy's needs.

evidence.note: Assessment that the government faces limited choices over the fleet.
Funding and staffing concerns, with personnel numbers identified as the crewing problem.

segments.summary: Expanding the Royal Navy would require funding and enough people to crew the fleet.
